analysis.one_liner: Requires social media apps to give minors safety tools, limit addictive design, and undergo annual audits.
analysis.headline: A House subcommittee advanced the Kids Online Safety Act to the full Energy and Commerce Committee on a 13–10 vote in December 2025; it has one sponsor, no cosponsors, and has not reached the House floor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require social media platforms to give users they know are minors tools to limit who contacts them, turn off addictive design features like infinite scrolling by default, and cap time on the app. Platforms would have to respond to reports of harm within 10 days, stop advertising drugs, tobacco, alcohol, and gambling to minors, pay for an independent audit every year, and face enforcement by the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general. It would also override state laws on the same subject, which could replace stricter rules some states have adopted with a federal floor that is lighter than the version that passed the Senate in the last Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Minors under 17 who use social media, and their parents. The bill defaults minors into the most protective privacy and safety settings a platform offers, limits compulsive-use features for them by default, gives parents tools to view settings and restrict time and purchases, requires a substantive response to harm reports within 10 days, and blocks ads for drugs, tobacco, cannabis, gambling, and alcohol aimed at known minors.

how_it_helps.text: Platforms must give users they know are minors easy-to-use safeguards, including limits on who can contact them and default limits on design features that drive compulsive use such as infinite scrolling, autoplay, and streak-style rewards.
Platforms must offer parents tools to view privacy settings, restrict time and purchases, and must enable those tools by default for users known to be children under 13.

Platforms must respond substantively to reports of harm to a minor within 10 days, sooner for imminent safety threats, and cannot advertise narcotic drugs, cannabis, tobacco, gambling, or alcohol to users they know are minors.

Every covered platform must undergo an annual independent third-party audit of its minor-safety practices and report results to the FTC, and violations are enforceable by the FTC and by state attorneys general.

analysis.who_pays: Social media and other user-content platforms, which must build and maintain safeguards, parental tools, reporting systems, and annual audits, and adjust their advertising practices. Indirectly, states give up their own lawmaking power on this subject, and all users may see product changes as platforms retool engagement features to avoid classifying them as compulsive-use drivers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Social media platforms and users' experience

drawbacks.text: The bill overrides all state laws 'relating to the provisions of this Act,' so states could no longer enforce their own, potentially stricter online-safety rules for minors once the federal floor takes effect.

Obligations apply only to users the platform 'knows' is a minor, and the bill explicitly bars requiring platforms to collect age information they do not already gather, so many teen users could fall outside the protections entirely.
There is no duty-of-care standard and no private right of action: families harmed by platform design cannot sue on their own; enforcement rests solely with the FTC and state attorneys general.

Parental tools let parents view — and, for users under 13, control — a minor's privacy and account settings and monitor time spent, which can enable surveillance of a young person's account and could be harmful in households where a minor's privacy or safety depends on it.
The core obligation is to adopt 'reasonable' policies scaled to each platform's size and technical feasibility, which gives large platforms wide latitude in how much they actually change.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are real but modest: default safety settings, parental tools, response deadlines, an advertising ban on age-restricted products, and annual audits would help some minors. The trade-offs are serious. Because the bill applies only where a platform already knows a user is a minor and forbids new age collection, many teenagers may be untouched by it. And its state-law preemption could leave the country with less protection than states like California have already enacted on their own, while the lack of a duty of care and a private right of action means harmed families have no direct remedy. On balance this is a lighter-touch version of online-safety regulation, closer to what platforms could live with than to the strictest proposals.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared its House subcommittee on a 13–10 vote on December 11, 2025 and now sits before the full Energy and Commerce Committee, which has not yet taken it up.

narrative.text: Rep. Gus Bilirakis introduced the bill on December 5, 2025 and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
It was referred the same day to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade, which held a markup on December 11, 2025.
The subcommittee voted 13–10 to forward an amended substitute to the full committee.
The bill has zero cosponsors as of the record provided.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No final winner yet. If the bill keeps advancing, major platforms gain a uniform federal standard and the preemption of stricter state laws; if it stalls, states keep their own rules and platforms face nothing new. Families of minors online have gained nothing so far.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No winner yet; platforms could gain uniform rules

for.name: Rep. Gus Bilirakis
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member

for.name: 13 members of the Energy and Commerce Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade Subcommittee
for.what_they_did: Voted to forward an amended substitute of the bill to the full committee on a 13–10 vote.

against.name: 10 members of the Energy and Commerce Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade Subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Voted no on forwarding the bill to the full committee.

against.name: Tech industry groups such as NetChoice
against.role: Trade associations representing major social media platforms
against.what_they_did: Campaigns against Kids Online Safety Act–style mandates, arguing they burden platforms and threaten free expression; the industry has historically lobbied against versions of this bill.

sides.party_line_note: The only recorded vote was the subcommittee's 13–10 on December 11, 2025, a close margin that suggests division, but the record does not break down the vote by party; the sole sponsor is a Republican with no cosponsors listed.

industries.note: The bill imposes compliance costs — default safeguards, parental tools, 10-day report responses, and annual third-party audits — but also hands platforms two wins: it preempts stricter state online-safety laws, and it omits the duty-of-care standard and private right of action that appeared in earlier versions of this legislation. The net result is a federal floor lighter than the toughest state rules.
Every covered platform must commission an annual independent third-party audit of its minor-safety practices, creating a recurring paid engagement for audit firms.

State AGs gain new authority to sue platforms for violations on behalf of residents, but lose the power to pass or enforce their own state laws on the same subject matter, capping how far any single state can go.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is at the full Energy and Commerce Committee after a close subcommittee vote, with a single sponsor and no cosponsors. Most House bills at this stage — especially ones this contested, with industry lobbying against them — never get a committee vote or a floor vote. If leadership decides child online safety is a priority this Congress, a negotiated version could move, but the lack of cosponsors in the first week and the 13–10 margin both point toward a slow, uncertain path.
